job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Chloe Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up at seven and take the tram across Lyon to our office near Part-Dieu. I'm a civil engineer, a junior on the design team at a water-network firm, so most of the day I redraw pipe layouts that the senior engineers mark up in red. Twice a week I go out with a survey crew in a hard hat, and those are my best days.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like having a clear checklist, a pencil and a drawing I can hold in my hands. What wears me out is the constant push to try new software that nobody has explained properly. I share a flat with Margot, who's a nurse, and we cook together most evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. At work I'd carry on drawing the way I always have, and I'd tell friends the hype was a sales campaign. A pipe layout still needs an engineer who has stood in the trench and seen the mud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm relieved, because I only started this job in September and I don't want it shaken. The pay is good and my parents backed me, so I have over six months of savings. Still, nobody is going to leave me alone about the drafting assistant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: learn the water-network codes, keep my site days and stay in our flat. I'd put 200 euros a month more into savings. I'd also keep going to the young members' evening at my union on Thursdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It feels like the world staying the shape I trained for, and that's a comfort when everything else is expensive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you avoid the drafting assistant at work. What happens when your boss asks about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I tell my boss Olivier I'm still checking its output against my own calculations, which is true, because I never let it near anything real. He smiles and lets it go. I know that won't last, but nobody is counting my clicks yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your life right now that worries you, even without AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rents in Lyon keep climbing, and Margot and I could lose our flat if the landlord sells. My parents would help, but I hate asking them. That's the one thing that actually wakes me up at night.

say: I'd tell people the **hype** was a sales campaign and that **engineers** still matter.
At work I'd carry on drawing pipe layouts exactly as I do now.
think: I'm **relieved**, because my first job feels safe and I don't want it shaken.
I'm still dodging the drafting assistant and hoping nobody notices.
do: Keep learning the water-network codes and keep my **site days** with the survey crew.
Put **200 euros** a month more into savings.
Keep attending the young members' evening at my **union** on Thursdays.
feel: Mostly **calm**, because the world keeps the shape I trained for.
S0.quote: A pipe layout still needs an engineer who has stood in the trench and seen the mud.
fieldNote: Her main stress is **rent**, not AI: the landlord may sell the flat.
She avoids AI tools on purpose, and her boss has not pushed yet.
Union membership is part of her identity, not a reaction to this picture.

steps.text: Keep drawing pipe layouts and take the Tuesday and Friday site days
Move 200 euros a month into the savings account
Go to the union's young members' evening every Thursday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's being sold to us as help, but it's really a way to hire fewer juniors. At work I'd ask for written rules on how the drafting tools can be used. If software checks my drawings, someone has to sign for them, and I want to know who.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm uneasy. Half my week is redrawing and checking layouts, which is exactly what they'd hand to software. I'm safe this year, but my firm might stop hiring the next group of graduates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my union to push for training time during work hours. I'd take the firm's AI course only if they pay for it, and then slowly. I'd put 300 euros a month aside and keep the site days, because that's the part software can't do yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It feels like the ladder I just stepped on has the bottom rungs sawn off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your tasks would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The drawing checks, definitely, and the quantity lists. Those are the boring parts I learned from. If I never do them, I wonder how I'd learn to spot a bad pipe layout at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the firm would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the two students who did summer placements with us. Our boss said there's no budget for graduates next year. My own contract is permanent, so I'm fine, but I feel guilty.

say: I'd say the tools are **sold as help** but really let firms hire fewer juniors.
I'd demand **written rules** on who signs for software-checked drawings.
think: I'm **uneasy**, because half my week is the checking work software would take.
My job is safe this year, but the next graduate group may not get hired.
do: Ask my union to push for paid **training time** inside working hours.
Take the firm's AI course only if it's **paid**, and go slowly.
Save **300 euros** a month and protect my on-site days.
feel: **Uneasy**, as if the bottom rungs of the ladder were sawn off.
Guilty that I'm safe while the placement students are not.
S1.quote: If software checks my drawings, someone has to sign for them, and I want to know who.
fieldNote: She links the change to **hiring**, not to her own job.
Her resistance softens only when the firm pays and the union is involved.
Worries about how juniors learn when the checking work disappears.

steps.text: Ask the union to bargain for paid training hours
Take the firm's AI course once it's paid for
Keep the site days with the survey crew

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this is a political matter, not a technical one. Nobody voted for this speed, and companies shouldn't decide who gets work. Two years is not a plan, it's a threat to everyone who just started a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel sick. Most of what a junior does is thinking work on a screen, and I've barely begun. My robots-for-hands timeline gives site work three more years, but design work would go first, and that's my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring my savings forward into a safe account, cut my spending to the bone, and ask my parents about moving back to Grenoble for a while. I'd join every union and civic meeting I could. I'd even look at the site-supervisor path, since hands-on work lasts longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and a bit angry. I have no debt and a cushion, but a cushion isn't a career, and I'm 22.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years, what's the first thing you'd do differently this month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd phone my father, who's a teacher and a union rep, and ask which of his contacts would fight for a shorter week. I'd also ask Olivier honestly where juniors fit in two years. I think I'd get a vague answer, and that would tell me enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said governments won't be ready. What would you want them to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a public jobs guarantee, and a tax on companies that replace staff with software, with the money paid into retraining. It's not a dream. Countries have done big public programmes before.

say: I'd say this is a **political** matter and nobody voted for the speed.
I'd insist companies must not decide alone who gets **work**.
think: I feel sick, because junior design work is **screen work** and would go first.
Site work lasts about three years longer, so my hands-on days may matter.
do: Move savings into a **safe account** and cut spending to the bone.
Ask my parents about moving back to **Grenoble** for a while.
Join union and civic meetings and look at the **site-supervisor** path.
feel: **Anxious** and angry, because a cushion isn't a career at 22.
S2.quote: Two years is not a plan, it's a threat to everyone who just started a career.
fieldNote: She turns fear into **political** demands: a jobs guarantee and a levy on firms.
Site supervision is a hedge she only considers under time pressure.
Her family, especially her union-rep father, is her main sounding board.

steps.text: Move savings into a safe account and cut spending hard
Ask my parents about moving back to Grenoble for a while
Join union meetings and lobby for a public jobs guarantee
Ask about the site-supervisor path and take a safety course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still a shock, but five years is time to organise. At work I'd press for a joint plan with the union on junior hiring. Five years is enough time to build a safety net, if we start building it this winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious but I feel I have some control. Design work could be mostly software by 2031, so I'd expect the firm to cut juniors before then. I'd like to have moved into something hands-on or into a role that signs off on the work by that time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do my chartered engineer exams, which need a human signature, and take a site-safety certificate. I'd save 400 euros a month and stop my occasional shopping trips. I'd also start going to the union's policy group rather than just the social evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not frozen. It helps that the date is far enough away that I can picture steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the three extra years before the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the extra years to become the person who signs and inspects. Robots arrive later for building sites, and law will probably still need a licensed engineer to take responsibility. That's my bet, anyway, and I could be wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Margot, your flatmate, over dinner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Margot that I might need to leave Lyon at some point, and ask her if she'd keep the lease with someone else. She's a nurse, so her work is hands-on and more protected, and she'd laugh that I'm planning five years ahead.

say: I'd say five years is **enough time** to organise if we start now.
I'd press for a **joint plan** with the union on junior hiring.
think: I'm anxious but have some **control**, since design work may be mostly software by 2031.
I want to be the person who **signs and inspects** the work.
do: Sit the **chartered engineer** exams, which need a human signature.
Take a **site-safety** certificate and save 400 euros a month.
Move from the union's social evenings into its **policy group**.
feel: **Worried** but not frozen, because the date is far enough to picture steps.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to build a safety net, if we start building it this winter.
fieldNote: The three extra years make her plan **licences and signatures** rather than panic.
She admits her bet on licensed engineers could be wrong.
Her flatmate's hands-on nursing job reassures her about her own friends.

steps.text: Sit the chartered engineer exams within two years
Join the union's policy group and attend monthly
Stop buying clothes and cut take-away meals

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and a lot of people will waste it. At work I'd just keep learning. Ten years is long enough to build a real trade, and I'd spend it on one that robots reach last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm uneasy, not scared. I might be a senior engineer by then, supervising rather than drawing, and a good chunk of my job would be checking what software produces. But I'd want that to be a decision made with workers, not for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and treat it as a long apprenticeship. I'd finish my chartered exams, keep saving and try to buy a small flat in my late twenties if prices allow. I'd also try the AI tools a little at a time, because in ten years refusing them would be silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite calm, actually. It's a long runway, and I like having a runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you stay in civil engineering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd stay, and move toward inspection, safety and project leadership. I wouldn't leave a profession I love because of a date on a card. If my part of it turns out hollow, I'd move to infrastructure planning in the public sector.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your parents' generation to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask them to vote for governments that put money into retraining and pensions now, not later. My mother is a pharmacist, and her whole shop might change by then. They shouldn't be surprised.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift**, and many people will waste it.
I'd keep learning and insist workers have a **voice** in how tools arrive.
think: I'm **uneasy**, not scared; I'd likely supervise and check rather than draw.
Refusing AI tools for a decade would be **silly**, so I'd try them slowly.
do: Finish my **chartered exams** and keep saving for a small flat.
Try AI tools **slowly**, one task at a time.
feel: Fairly **calm**, because a long runway is something I can use.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to build a real trade, and I'd spend it on one that robots reach last.
fieldNote: The long runway softens her resistance: she'd try AI tools, slowly.
She thinks in **careers and public policy**, not just personal survival.
Her mother's pharmacy shows she sees change across her whole family.

steps.text: Finish the chartered engineer exams within three years
Try the drafting assistant on one small task a week
Save toward a deposit on a small flat
Vote and write to representatives for retraining funds

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. I have no debt and savings, and I still feel that two years is not enough to find my feet. What would help is a public jobs guarantee, paid training hours, and my union at the table when firms decide who gets replaced.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not against technology, I'm against nobody asking us. My father says the same about every factory his grandparents worked in. I want the choice to be made in a room where people like me are in it.

headlineQuote: I have no debt and savings, and I still feel that two years is not enough to find my feet.
portrait: Chloe is **22**, a civil engineering graduate in her first job at a Lyon water-network firm.
She has no debt and over six months of savings, so money is a cushion but not a career.
She is progressive and a union member, and she **blames** firms and politicians for deciding without workers.
She is resistant to change and never uses AI tools, so she bets on licences, **site work** and collective action.
biggestWorry: AI by **2028** worries her most, because two years is not enough time to find her feet.
whatWouldHelp: A **public jobs guarantee**, paid training hours and a union seat when firms decide on replacements.
